captions.text: At 350 kilometers per hour, a bullet train
turns a tunnel into a cannon. The air
ahead cannot escape through the narrow gap. It
compresses into a moving wall, then fires out
of the far portal.
400 meters away, windows rattle and glass can
crack. The train never touches anything. The air
does all of it. Engineers call this tunnel
boom. The obvious fix is a sharper nose,
but a needle shape adds weight and crosswind
instability.
The real fix came from a bird that
dives without a splash. A beak solved a
pressure problem.
Inside a long tunnel, the pressure ahead of
a fast train can climb to several kilopascals.
That is enough force to flex steel and
shake concrete. The pressure wave steepens as it
runs, then reaches the portal and radiates into
open air. Low frequencies bend around buildings, so
the boom arrives hundreds of meters away. Sound
crosses that distance in about one second. Residents
hear a thud, then a crack. The engine
is innocent. The tunnel mouth is the weapon.
The pressure does not need a crash to
cause damage. It only needs a fast train
and a narrow tube.
A Kingfisher enters water without a splash because
its beak changes shape gradually. Engineer Ijinakatsu copied
that curve and stretched a Sheen Khan Sen
nose to about 15 meters. The air no
longer meets a wall. It meets a gentle
squeeze. The pressure peak drops, and the tunnel
boom softens. The 500 series cut energy use
and noise with reports of about 30% less
noise. The train still compresses the air. It
just stops fighting it.
The invisible wall was reshaped, not removed. The
next wall is underwater, where bubbles collapse at
1,100 atmospheres.
